utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-94-2-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Before we start, let me first make sure that everybody can follow the proceedings. Mr. Nikolic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Under the Rules, we have today a Status Conference. It's a special Status Conference to that end that - and I have to tell this for reasons of transparency - initially it was aimed at having a plea agreement, but all the intents failed to come to such an agreement until now. We have, however, a new indictment, the third amended indictment. And following Rule 50 of our Statute and of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, when new charges are included a further appearance shall be held as soon as practicable to enable the accused to enter a plea on the new charges. And this will form the first part of today's hearing. Let me take the opportunity to thank the parties, both parties, for all their efforts to streamline this case. Initially we had a case including 88 counts. Today when we will hear this indictment, we have four counts only. But also for reasons of transparency, it has to be emphasised that nothing has changed with the factual basis. It is only a new assessment and streamlining of the legal assessment of the case. And I think that's the most important development. I thank you, because we're all aware how precious and good the time of the judiciary is and that it's in the interest of the one having mandated us, the international taxpayer, to come as soon as possible to a solution and not to expound on unnecessary charges. So when having heard the plea of Mr. Nikolic related to the new charges, then we have to decide, and of course it depends on the outcome of his pleas, whether we have to set a date for trial for September or set a date for a sentencing hearing later. May I ask the Defence: Did you have the possibility to discuss this new document with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: If it please, Your Honour, yes, the opportunity has been given. The indictment has been translated into B/C/S, and the defendant has had an opportunity to read it and is now content to enter pleas to that indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nikolic, before the indictment will be read out, it's my obligation once again to tell you that it's your right to remain silent. No inference to your disadvantage can be drawn if you remain totally silent. The only inference that can be drawn can be found in Rule 62 of our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, where you can read that "If the accused fails to enter a plea in a further appearance, the Judge shall enter a plea of not guilty on the accused's behalf." But I have to warn you at the same time that everything you may say in the courtroom may be used even against you in evidence. This part of the admonition is mandatory under the Rules and under the fundamental principles of criminal procedure. However, it is only fair to tell you about the other side of the same coin. With respect especially to your case, I have once again to tell you that as a general rule respected in all courtrooms on this globe that any kind of cooperation would be of advantage for an accused. You, Mr. Nikolic, are best placed to know what really happened between June 1992 and September 1992. You have had the chance during the last three years to assess in general terms the evidence available. Therefore, Mr. Nikolic, it is for you to decide which avenue you take, to make use of the right to remain silent or to cooperate. It is for you to plea guilty or not guilty. You are aware about the consequences. May I ask you, did you understand this admonition, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then may I ask Madam Registrar to read out the third amended indictment of June 23, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, pursuant to her authority under Article 18 of the Statute of the Tribunal, charges: Dragan Nikolic, also known as Jenki, with crimes against humanity as set forth below: The accused, Dragan Nikolic, born on 26 April 1957, is from the town of Vlasenica, Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before the war, he worked at the Alpro aluminium factory in Vlasenica. He lived with his family on Zarka Vukavica Street in the Krusevik section of Vlasenica. From at least early June 1992 until about 30 September, 1992, Dragan Nikolic was commander of Susica detention camp in Vlasenica. Individual criminal responsibility. Article 7(1) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Dragan Nikolic is individually criminally responsible pursuant to Article 7(1) for planning, instigating, ordering, committing or otherwise aiding and abetting in the planning, preparation, or execution of all crimes charged in the indictment. The charges: Count 1, persecutions. From at least early June 1992 until about 30 September 1992 Dragan Nikolic persecuted the Muslim and non-Serb detainees at Susica camp on political, racial, and religious grounds. Dragan Nikolic persecuted Muslim and non-Serb detainees at the Susica camp by subjecting them to murders, rapes, and torture as charged specifically in the indictment. In addition, Dragan Nikolic persecuted Muslims and non-Serb detainees by participating in sexual violence directed at women at the Susica camp as set forth in paragraph 20 and 21 of the indictment. As part of the persecutions, Dragan Nikolic detained Muslim and non-Serbs at the Susica camp and assisted in the forcible transfer of those at the camp from the Vlasenica municipality. At the end of June 1992, large numbers of the male detainees were transferred from the camp to the larger Batkovic detention camp near Bijelina in north-eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of the women and children detainees were transferred either to Kladanj or Cerska in Bosnian-Muslim controlled territory. As part of the persecutions, Dragan Nikolic subjected detainees to an atmosphere of terror created by the murders, beatings, sexual violence and other physical and mental abuse of detainees and to inhumane living conditions by being deprived of adequate food, water, medical care, sleeping and toilet facilities. As a result, detainees suffered severe psychological and physical trauma. Dragan Nikolic participated in creating and maintaining this atmosphere of terror and the inhumane conditions. By his participation in the acts or omissions described in paragraph 3(6) Dragan Nikolic is individually criminally responsible for: Count 1: Persecutions on political, racial and religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(h) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 2, murder. Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. One evening between about 13 June 1992 and about 24 June 1992 Dragan Nikolic and other guards at Susica camp entered the hangar building and called out Durmo Handzic and Asim Zildzic. After taking them outside the building Dragan Nikolic and the guards subjected Durmo Handzic, and Asim Zildzic to severe physical abuse, including punching, kicking, and beatings with weapons such as lengths of wood lasting for at least 45 minutes, during which time the two men repeatedly begged for the beating to stop. When the beating concluded, both detainees were brought back to the hangar. Asim Zildzic died shortly after returning. The following morning upon the order of Dragan Nikolic, two detainees buried Asim Zildzic. Later that morning Dragan Nikolic entered the hangar and approached Durmo Handzic. Although Handzic was in severe agony from being beaten the night before, Dragan Nikolic demanded information regarding Durmo Handzic's son. Durmo Handzic died shortly after his encounter and was buried that day by other detainees. Rasid Ferhatbegovic, Muharem Kolarevic, Dzevad Saric and Ismet Zekic. During the night of 23 and 24 June 1992, Dragan Nikolic entered the hangar and ordered Muharem Kolarevic and Dzevad Saric to be taken outside. Sometime after that, other guards removed Ismet "Musa" Zekic also from the hangar. For approximately 30 minutes after the men were taken from the hangar, detainees inside heard cries of pain and then gunshots that came from a location close to the hangar. After the gunshots were heard, a guard called two detainees from the hangar and ordered them to dispose of the bodies of Muharem Kolarevic and Zvevad Saric behind the hangar. Dragan Nikolic ordered the two detainees to wash away the blood on the ground where the deceased had been beaten. After attempting to wash away the blood, the two detainees waited outside the hangar. As Dragan Nikolic sat inside the nearby guardhouse, the two men watched the same guard who had called them out to the hangar shoot and kill Ismet Zekic. Shortly after Ismet Zekic was killed, Dragan Nikolic and the guard who had shot Zekic entered the hangar with some local police. The police pointed at Rasid Ferhatbegovic and asked if he was the one who was running away. The guard who had shot Ismet Zekic said yes. Rasid Ferhatbegovic was then taken outside and shortly thereafter the other prisoners heard one shot. Early the next morning, Dragan Nikolic entered the hangar and again called out the two detainees who had disposed of the bodies the day before. They went to the area of the camp that was being used as a toilet and found the body of Muharem Kolarevic slumped over a fence caught in a wire. The guard who had shot Ismet Zekic the day before then shot Kolarevic again. The two prisoners then took the body of Muharem Kolarevic to where they had left the bodies the previous evening and there they saw the body of Rasid Ferhatbegovic with a bullet hole in the centre of his forehead. Ismet Dedic. On or about 6 July 1992, Dragan Nikolic took Ismet Dedic out of the hangar at Susica camp and closed the door behind them. Detainees inside the hall then heard Ismet Dedic scream. A few minutes later Dragan Nikolic directed two detainees to drag Ismet Dedic inside the hangar where the other detainees could see that Ismet Dedic's body was covered in blood. His body was barely recognisable and he appeared to have suffered serious injuries. Ismet Dedic died shortly thereafter. His body was placed in a plastic bag and removed from other detainees. Mevludin Hatunic. Mevludin Hatunic, his wife and daughter were detained in Susica camp in early July 1992. Between about 3 July and 7 July 1992, while detained in the camp, Mevludin Hatunic offered his house to a Serb in exchange for moving his family out of the area. Hatunic was then permitted to leave the camp to arrange the transfer of the house. Upon his return, Dragan Nikolic accused Hatunic of having told the Serb to whom he had given his house that Hatunic would wait for his opportunity to get even. That evening, because he had allegedly made such a statement, Dragan Nikolic beat Mevludin Hatunic. The next morning Dragan Nikolic beat Mevludin Hatunic again until Mevludin Hatunic lost consciousness. Later that evening Dragan Nikolic returned and finding that Mevludin Hatunic had regained consciousness beat him a third time. A short time later Mevludin Hatunic died as a result of the beatings. His body was placed in a plastic bag and was removed from the hangar by other detainees. Galib Music. From about the second week of July, 1992 over a second day period -- a seven-day period, Dragan Nikolic beat Galib Music, a 60-year-old detainee, by, among other things, kicking him and beating him with a metal pipe. During the beatings, Dragan Nikolic accused Galib Music of asking a Muslim organisation to come to expel the Serbs from Vlasenica. Each time Dragan Nikolic beat Galib Music, Music lost consciousness and after approximately seven days Galib Music died. By his participation in the acts and omissions described in paragraphs 8 through 18 in relation to Durmo Handzic, Asim Zildzic, Rasid Ferhatbegovic, Muharem Kolarevic, Dzevad Saric, Ismet Zekic, Ismet Dedic, Mevludin Hatunic and Galib Music, Dragan Nikolic is individually criminally responsibility for: Count 2: Murder, a crime against humanity, punishable numbered Article 5(a) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 3, sexual violence. From early June until about 15 September 1992, many female detainees at Susica camp were subjected to sexual assaults including rapes and degrading physical and verbal abuse. Dragan Nikolic personally removed and otherwise facilitated the removal of female detainees from the hangar which he knew were for the purpose of rapes and other sexually abusive conducts. The sexual assaults were committed by camp guards, special forces, local soldiers, and other men. Female detainees were sexually assaulted at various locations, such as the guardhouse, the houses surrounding the camp, at the Panorama Hotel, a military headquarters, and at locations where such women were taken to perform forced labour. Dragan Nikolic allowed female detainees, including girls and elderly women, to be verbally subjected to humiliating sexual threats in the presence of other detainees in the hangar. Dragan Nikolic facilitated the removal of female detainees by allowing guards, soldiers, and other males to have access to these women on a repetitive basis and by otherwise encouraging the sexually abusive conduct. By his aiding and abetting in the conduct described in paragraph 20 and 21, in relation to female detainees in the Susica camp, Dragan Nikolic is individually criminally responsible for: Count 3: Rape, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(G) of the Statute of the Tribunal. Count 4, torture. Fikret "Cice" Arnaut. From about 1 June to about 18 July 1992, Dragan Nikolic beat Fikret "Cice" Arnaut, by kicking him, stomping on him, and punching him with metal knuckles on his fists. The beatings took place both inside and outside the hangar. Several of the beatings took place in a corner of the hangar known as the punishment corner. On one occasion Dragan Nikolic came into the hangar and told Fikret Arnaut to kneel on the floor, put his hands behind his head, and tilt his head back. Dragan Nikolic then put a bayonet in his mouth and asked him about his brothers, who Dragan Nikolic claimed had joined a group of the Ustasha. Later that same day, two men came to the hangar and took Fikret Arnaut outside. When Fikret Arnaut returned, he had been beaten severely and was bleeding from his mouth. Shortly thereafter, Dragan Nikolic came to Fikret Arnaut in the hangar and said words to the effect, "What? They did not beat you enough; if it had been me, you would not be able to walk. They are not as well trained to beat people as I am." On one occasion, Dragan Nikolic took Fikret Arnaut outside the hangar and beat Fikret Arnaut with metal knuckles. Fikret Arnaut fell to the ground and Dragan Nikolic kicked his rib and back around the kidney area. During this beating, Dragan Nikolic accused Fikret Arnaut of organising the Muslims. On a subsequent occasion, Dragan Nikolic approached Fikret Arnaut in the hangar and said words to the effect, "I can't believe how an animal like this can't die. He must have two hearts." Dragan Nikolic then beat Fikret Arnaut again and stomped on his chest. Sead Ambeskovic and Hajrudin Osmanovic. On 11 June 1992, Sead Ambeskovic was arrested in Vlasenica. Police first interrogated him and took him to the Susica camp. Once in the camp, Dragan Nikolic and others beat Sead Ambeskovic, using axe handles, iron bars, and rifle butts. In the morning of 14 June 1992, guards took Sead Ambeskovic and Hajrudin Osmanovic from the hangar. The two men were ordered to kneel with their hands behind their heads. Dragan Nikolic asked them where their weapons were and to identify others who had weapons. During the interrogation, Dragan Nikolic and others then beat them with iron bars, wooden bats, and rifle butts for approximately one and one half hours. As a result of this beating, the back of Sead Ambeskovic's head was cut. Four teeth on the left side of his mouth were knocked out and three ribs were broken. On or about 16 June 1992, Dragan Nikolic again called Sead Ambeskovic and Hajrudin Osmanovic out of the hangar. Once outside, Dragan Nikolic demanded to know if they had weapons and who else had weapons. Dragan Nikolic and two other guards immediately began beating them with bats for 10 to 15 minutes. On 3 July 1992, Hajrudin Osmanovic was taken from the Susica camp to perform forced labour; he has never been seen since. Suad Mahmutovic. From about 13 June to about 3 July 1992, Suad Mahmutovic suffered frequent sometimes daily beatings by Dragan Nikolic at Susica camp. Dragan Nikolic beat Suad Mahmutovic with iron bars, rifle butts, and rubber tubing with led inside. During one beating, seven of Suad Mahmutovic's ribs were broken. On a separate occasion, Dragan Nikolic kicked Suad Mahmutovic in the face with his boot which caused a cut that left permanent scars. On one occasion, Dragan Nikolic placed a cocked pistol inside Suad Mahmutovic's mouth. Dragan Nikolic tried to force Suad Mahmutovic to admit that his neighbour had a weapon, but Suad Mahmutovic refused. Dragan Nikolic then pulled the trigger but the gun was not loaded. Redzo Cakisic was arrested on 2 June 1992 and taken to Susica camp. Upon arrival, Dragan Nikolic and other guards searched him. He was then taken to the hangar where with other detainees he was ordered to line up and lean against the wall with his hands behind his back. Dragan Nikolic then hit Redzo Cakisic and other detainees with his rifle butt and kicked him with his boots. Approximately ten days later, Dragan Nikolic called Redzo Cakisic from the hangar during the night. Two men were waiting outside with Dragan Nikolic. Nikolic said to them words to the effect, "Here, I brought you something for dinner." The two men who were not camp guards hit Redzo Cakisic in the back with rifle butts and kicked him in the stomach and sides. During this beating, Dragan Nikolic was approximately 5 metres away in the guardhouse. The beating continued for about 20 minutes. By his participation in the acts and omissions described in paragraphs 23 to 34, in relation to Fikret "Cice" Arnaut, Sead Ambeskovic, Hajrudin Osmanovic, Suad Mahmutovic, and Redzo Cakisic, Dragan Nikolic is individually criminally responsible for: Count 4: Torture, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(f) of the Statute of the Tribunal. General legal allegations. All acts or omissions charged as crimes against humanity occurred during an armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and were related to a widespread or systematic attack directed against the civilian population, specifically the Muslim and non-Serb population of the Vlasenica municipality. Additional facts. The municipality of Vlasenica is in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina, approximately 50 kilometres west of the Serbian border and approximately 120 kilometres north-east of Sarajevo. According to the 1991 census, the municipality had approximately 33.817 citizens of whom approximately 55 per cent were Muslim, 43 per cent were Serb, and 2 per cent were described as other. The town of Vlasenica is located within the municipality of the same name. In 1991, the town of Vlasenica had approximately 7.500 citizens, approximately 65 per cent of whom were Muslim and 35 per cent were Serb. In January 1992, Serbs from Vlasenica in eight neighbouring municipalities declared the area to be the "Birac Autonomous Region" within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Tensions increased in the spring of 1992 with the referendum on the proposed independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. About 21 of April, 1992 Serb forces took over the town of Vlasenica and declared it to be the Serbian town -- declared it to be a Serbian town. JNA soldiers, including soldiers purporting to be from the Novi Sad Corps from Serbia, the paramilitary forces and local military soldiers participated in the takeover. During the day, police vehicles drove around Vlasenica town and issued an ultimatum over loudspeakers for Muslims to turn in their weapons. The Muslim population complied with the ultimatum and did not resist. Once the Serbs took control of the municipality, the Crisis Staff, (Krisni Stab) administered the town and appointed Serbs to all of the official positions. Local Serb men were mobilised and took over military responsibilities from the JNA forces. Among other things, local Serb military forces guarded important facilities and later were formed into companies and used to search surrounding woods for armed Muslims. After the takeover, conditions for Muslims and other non-Serbs in the municipality deteriorated. The Serb authorities fired Muslims and other non-Serbs from their jobs and limited their withdrawal of funds from banks. The Serb authorities did not permit the Muslims and other non-Serbs to travel without special passes. Muslim men were frequently arrested and brought to the police station for interrogation. Beatings and murders sometimes accompanied the interrogations. Many Muslims and other non-Serbs fled to the Vlasenica area, and beginning in May 1992 and continuing until September 1992 those Muslims and other non-Serbs were -- who had remained were either forcibly expelled or arrested. By September 1992, virtually no Muslims or non-Serbs remained in Vlasenica. The Serb forces initially held the arrested Muslims and other Serbs either at a local school or the local prison of Vlasenica. In approximately late May or early June 1992, the Serb forces established a detention camp at Susica, the main detention facility in Vlasenica area, and sent the arrested Muslims and non-Serbs there. The Susica camp was run by the military and the local police militia. The camp guards were generally soldiers from the local area. Susica camp was located approximately 1 kilometre from the town of Vlasenica, in a military facility that had previously been used for storage of military equipment. Men, women, and children were kept in the camp. However, the women and children generally stayed for only short periods of time before being forcibly transferred to nearby Muslim areas. Before being forcibly transferred, non-Serbs usually had to sign a document stating that they were leaving the area voluntarily and that they were giving up their possessions. Susica camp consisted of two main buildings, a warehouse or hangar, 50 metres by 30 metres, which was used to house the detainees, and a second smaller building which was used for storage of the equipment. There was also a small house used by the guards and commander of the camp to interrogate detainees when they arrived. Between late May and October 1992, as many as 8.000 Muslim civilians and other non-Serbs from Vlasenica and the surrounding villages were detained in the hangar in the Susica camp. The number of detainees in the hangar at any one time varied but was generally between 300 and 500 detainees. The building was severely overcrowded, detainees were not provided with anything to sleep on, toilet facilities were limited, and there were no showers. The food provided was sparse and often spoiled. The guards brutally beat the detainees on a daily basis. Many detainees died from the beatings by the guards. Many of the detained women were subjected to sexual assaults, including rape. Camp guards or other men who were allowed to enter the camp frequently took women out of the hangar at night. When the women entered, they were often in a traumatised state and other detainees observed that the women were distraught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Nikolic, under the Rules, we have to be satisfied that what we expect now, your plea, will be made voluntarily and at the same time informed. May I therefore ask you: Was there any pressure exercised on you by one of the parties or by any third persons, or do you have reasons to believe that such pressure was exercised on you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you furthermore: Did you understand this third amended indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did. I did understand it fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then finally, I have to repeat that what I had stated already beforehand, only that you are really aware of the importance of what will happen now. I stated beforehand that it is of course your right to plea not guilty or to plea guilty. It is your voluntary decision, as you just stated. But you also have to be aware of the consequences. In all likelihood, today it will be the last chance for you in this case, pending now for three years, that if established beyond a reasonable doubt in the final assessment the then-Trial Chamber to which this case will be assigned can take into account a plea as a mitigating factor. You have to be aware of this. May I ask you: Do you want to discuss this question once more with your Defence team, or are you prepared to enter a plea to the charges right now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have spoken to my counsel, and I am prepared to enter a plea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Nikolic, may I ask you what is your plea related to count 1, persecutions on political, racial, religious grounds, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(H) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Count 2, murder, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(a) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Count 3, rape, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(g) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And finally, count 4, torture, a crime against humanity, punishable under Article 5(f) of the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Madam Registrar, we have noted that Mr. Nikolic has entered a plea of not guilty to all the counts of the third amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We have now to discuss how to proceed. It was not foreseen that we would have a hearing that late on Friday afternoon. Unfortunately, one of our colleagues is not able to continue sitting. May I, therefore, ask the parties whether they agree that we continue the hearing after a short break under Rule 15 bis in the composition of two Judges only. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no objections to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no objections nor observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The accused himself?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the trial stays adjourned until half past 4.00, and immediately after that we will continue our discussion on the continuation and especially setting a date for trial. The trial stays adjourned. --- Break taken at 4.18 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. As I said at the beginning of this hearing, due to the fact that Mr. Nikolic is in the Detention Unit now for -- now about three years, it's mandatory to start immediately as soon as practicable and feasible with the trial as such. Therefore, I have to ask the parties: What is from your point of view an obstacle to start the trial? I'm aware there are still two motions pending, the one on taking depositions and the one on protective measures. I'll come back to this later. I take it that the pre-trial briefs have been filed with all the necessary accompanying documents. Is this correct? May I ask the Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, subject of course to anything that comes to light between now and the trial date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Prosecution. Do you see any obstacles to set a date for trial for September this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for giving me this opportunity. I can assure the Trial Chamber that in respect of pre-trial preparations, everything that need be done has been done. So we are quite comfortable with a date in September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the date in September for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the Defence is ready in principle to start the trial as soon as practicable after the summer recess. I have a -- a pre-existing commitment on the -- from the 17th to the 19th of September inclusive with the United Kingdom Judicial Studies Board, which would be impossible at this stage to -- to break without causing immense difficulties for a lot of people. Those three dates apart, three days apart, there are no other obstacles in the diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This shouldn't be a real obstacle. So let us now turn to the open motions. I think priority has to be given to the questions of depositions to be taken. We have in front of us the request from 28 February 2003. The reason why this was not yet decided was that there was a realistic chance to come to an agreement. But this has failed, and now we are confronted with this question. I have this document before me. May I ask the Defence team: Do you want to comment on this motion? Do you see any obstacle to take deposition as foreseen in this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, during the short recess, this matter was discussed together with the members of the Prosecutor's team in court, and we have tentatively identified the first working week of September as being a -- a possible week to do that, of course with the Trial Chamber's leave and consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But in principle, no obstacle taking depositions, related to the evidence mentioned in this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecution agrees that this could be done no later than the first week of September? Would this be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It is correct. My learned friend stated that he had discussed it with us, and we are in agreement that it could be done even the first week of September, this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us now turn to a second motion, that is, the Prosecution motion on protective measures. I can't go into any details, because it's for good reasons filed confidentially. That's a motion of 3 June 2003. We already received the answer concluding accordingly, "The Defence are content to leave the matter of protective measures to the discretion of the Trial Chamber." Based on the experience of previous cases, I think it's not foreseeable whether or not one would need additional protective measures or the other way around, that one would not need. May I ask, therefore, the Defence: Do you stick to your submission that you are prepared to leave this matter to the discretion of the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. The point is simple: The Defence do not concede that the matters contained in the motion are necessarily true. That's not the test. The test is whether or not the Prosecutor is acting bona fide in seeking such measures on the basis that they may be true. And on that basis, we do not seek to place any obstacle in the way of the Trial Chamber's discretion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber has conferred on this issue beforehand and hereby grants the motion of 3 June 2003. May I ask the Prosecution: Do you see any other obstacles or necessary prerequisites in order to start the case as envisaged for September?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. Your Honour is asking me about only on that aspect or in respect of any other matters that I have to raise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You may raise all the matters you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In order that we can come to the conclusion that we set a date for trial for September this year. So please address all the questions you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour. Your Honour made reference at the commencement of the proceedings today in respect of the indictment that was filed, the third amended indictment. And Your Honour was pleased to compliment the Prosecution and the Defence for getting the indictment done in that way. I thank Your Honour for the compliments paid. I'm sure my learned friend will acknowledge the compliments. But I have to make a brief reference to that, as to how it came about. Your Honour knows as to how it came about. And my learned friend also knows. So it may be necessary. I don't say that it will become necessary. The amendments were done for a particular reason, and it may be necessary for us to think over -- we have not yet thought over the present indictment -- to make some motion in the near future, in respect of that. I do not want to commit myself at this stage. But thinking of the reasons that prompted the making of the amendments, I am making this submission at this stage. Yes. That's what -- that's about all that I wanted to say about the indictment. There is another matter which I would make reference to maybe towards the end of the proceedings today. I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for purposes of clarification, we heard the plea of Mr. Nikolic a moment ago, and it goes without saying that when we asked Madam Registrar to read out the indictment, the third amended indictment, that we already beforehand accepted this third amended indictment. And I only mention it that it's confirmed and also reflected on the transcript. So we want to avoid any unnecessary filings; and therefore, please take this decision now already as an oral decision. Furthermore, I think it would be more than appropriate not once again to try to amend the indictment. I think the factual basis as it stands now is clear. It accurately reflects what seems to be the Prosecutor's case. And when changing or amending the indictment another time, we run the risk that maybe for good reasons, the Defence may refer to Rule 50(C), and this would postpone the start of trial another time. Having said this, may I ask the Defence that the Defence team and at the same time on behalf of the accused the Defence team waives the right of having a further period of 30 days in which to file preliminary motions pursuant to Rule 72 in respect of the new charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: The temptation is enormous. In practical terms, my answer is thank you but no thank you, Your Honour. We do not wish to file any further preliminary motions, and therefore we waive the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it would be adequate in return for the Prosecution to stick to the third amended indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for the advice. I did not say that I'm committing myself to an amendment. It was just a matter of considering because of the circumstances. That's all that I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understood your message very well. Thank you. May I then ask the Defence: Do you need anything in preparation of the case? Do you want to address any other issue in this Status Conference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Not at this stage, Your Honour. I am well aware that if I needed to address this Trial Chamber urgently as to anything that I would receive the same courtesy and cooperation that we've had hitherto, for which I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May I then finally ask - and this is one of the purposes of a Status Conference - Mr. Nikolic in person: Do you have actually any health problems or do you have any complaints about your situation in the United Nations Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no remarks to make with regard to the detention. I can say that I am very pleased that my trial will start, considering that it's been three years that I've been in detention. As far as health is concerned, I have no health problems. I can't say I'm very well. I can't say I'm fairing poorly. As far as the conditions of detention are concerned, everything is normal, there are no problems whatsoever. So the behaviour towards me has been the same from the beginning. As far as the health protection, the food, detention conditions, everything is fine as far as I'm concerned, at least. That's all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I thank you for this clear statement. Then the final issue is: We have to plan this case. We have to ask the President to ask the Secretary-General of the United Nations to appoint and assign Ad Litem Judges to this concrete case. And for this purpose, we have to know with the clarity that is possible to date how long will the case take. May I first ask the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Your Honour, the outer limit that I can mention is just five weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in terms of worst case and best case thinking, what would be the range?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Four to five -- four to five weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And for the Defence? I know it's more difficult for the Defence, because they haven't heard the Prosecutor's case. But I think you have an overview of the case. Mr. Morrison, may I ask you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: My assessment is that on the figures that have been given by my learned friend, this case could be concluded within two full working months, that is, something in the order of eight or nine weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what would be the time you would need? We have to count first of all the weeks needed for the Prosecutor's case. In all likelihood, 98 bis motion - I don't know whether -- it's not an invitation to file a 98 bis motion, not to be misunderstood. But what would be the time that you would need for your case, that we can add -- normally, iudex non calculat, a Judge doesn't count. But we want to count and we have to count today. What's your case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: I still anticipate that without -- as long as we do not have breaks so that we have a continuous flow of normal five working -- five normal working days per week, that this case can be concluded in a total of eight or nine weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Including the Prosecutor's case; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Including the Prosecutor's case. I mean, I am -- I have been in court before in the appellate proceedings with my learned friend, Mr. Yapa. I know the nature of his advocacy and operation. I think he begins to know mine. We do not waste time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I speak also on behalf of my colleague, Judge Mumba, that we appreciate to hear this clear words, and we know where we are. And as soon as practicable - you have heard what is necessary before we can provide you with the exact dates - we will let you know as soon as possible when the trial will start. It will start in September. Any other issues to be raised by one of the parties or the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: There is one special matter that I wish to raise. It will take only two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: May I move that we move into private session, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Yapa, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. YAPA
utterances.text: Sorry. I wish to mention the appearances of the Prosecution. It is as of last time. But the appearances: Myself, Upawansa Yapa; Ms. Patricia Sellers; Mr. William Smith; and our case manager for today's proceedings, Mr. David Bruff. I thank Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, I didn't want to repeat this. It changes from Trial Chamber to Trial Chamber, but I take it the appearances of the -- for the Defence were the same? If we have now the names from the side of the Prosecution, we also should have reflected your names on the transcript. If you could be so kind, Mr. Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISON
utterances.text: Your Honour, sometimes at the end of a working week I'm not entirely sure what my name is, but to the best of my recollection and having looked inside the label of my jacket, it's Howard Morrison, lead counsel for Mr. Nikolic, leading my very able co-counsel, Tanja Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for understanding this. That's a question of equality of arms. Normally I wouldn't do this at the end of the session, because I know everybody knows who is here during this Status Conference. I take it there are no other issues to be addressed today, and this concludes today's hearing. Thank you. And I wish everybody a nice weekend.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the Status Conference adjourned at
